observation: Cloud providers offer spot instances at typically 3–10× cheaper prices than on-demand instances, but spot instances are preemptible and their availability is highly volatile, varying strongly across zones and over time; availability can change from 100% to 0% within hours. Many workloads accept this uncertainty by checkpointing or re-executing, yet deadline-sensitive applications—such as incorporating new user data into an AI recommendation model or making timely trading decisions—cannot tolerate spot preemptions and therefore rely on expensive on-demand instances, trading cost for predictability. Thus it was unclear how deadline-bound jobs could safely exploit cheap spot resources without missing their deadlines.

solution.idea: Prior work draws a sharp line between cheap spot capacity and deadline safety. Transparent checkpointing such as DMTCP makes a preempted job resumable but gives no deadline bound; Borg-style scheduling meets hard completion targets only by placing jobs in a guaranteed class that is protected from preemption; SpotServe shows that moving revocation handling into the application runtime can make latency-sensitive serving work on spot, but it requires workload-specific state migration and tight coupling. The observation is that a deadline-bound job does not need every second of its execution to be protected. What it needs is that, at every instant, the work that has already been made durable through a checkpoint can still be finished on guaranteed on-demand capacity by the deadline. The uncheckpointed work currently being executed on a spot instance is speculative: if the spot instance is revoked, that speculative work is lost, but it must not be able to push the job past its deadline. The core insight is therefore to convert the deadline guarantee from a property of the execution class into a property of the checkpoint-protected progress curve. A job may run cheaply on spot for as long as the last durable checkpoint remains rescuable by on-demand within the deadline; as soon as the remaining time would not suffice for one more protected checkpoint and a subsequent fallback, the scheduler promotes the job into a Borg-like guaranteed on-demand class and restores the latest snapshot. This approach gives a hard deadline guarantee that is independent of spot price or availability forecasts, while still using spot resources whenever they are available before the point of no return. It differs from the prior alternatives by making the fallback automatic, generic, and scheduler-driven: DMTCP supplies transparent checkpointing, SpotServe supplies the revocation-watcher idea, and Borg supplies the guaranteed rescue queue, but no job is required to run exclusively on on-demand unless its checkpoint-protected slack has actually run out. The key design trade-off is checkpointing overhead versus safety margin: more frequent checkpoints shrink the amount of work lost on a spot revocation and allow more aggressive spot use, but they consume time and storage; the controller therefore sets each spot lease no longer than the leftover rescue slack minus the time needed for a checkpoint. I rejected a purely probabilistic availability model because spot availability can collapse from 100% to 0 in hours and a hard deadline cannot be based on predictions; I rejected always-on on-demand shadow instances because they double cost; and I rejected application-specific migration because it does not generalize to the wide class of deadline-bound jobs that the observation describes.
solution.implementation: The system consists of an admission controller, a centralized lease scheduler, per-instance spot agents running DMTCP, and a guaranteed on-demand rescue queue managed as a Borg-style protected class. Each job j is described by a total amount of work W_j measured in on-demand compute time on a reference instance type, a deadline D_j, and the measured fixed overhead O_j of a rescue path, meaning the time to launch an on-demand instance, attach the persistent state store, and restore a DMTCP checkpoint. The scheduler also profiles C_j, the worst-case time to take a full DMTCP checkpoint and commit it to durable storage for this job. The controller stores for each job a protected progress p_j, which is the amount of completed work contained in the latest committed checkpoint. At admission, with p_j = 0 and current time t, the controller accepts the job only if t + O_j + W_j / r_on <= D_j, where r_on is the on-demand processing rate; otherwise even a fresh on-demand run cannot meet the deadline and no spot usage can help. For an accepted job, the controller computes the latest rescue request time R_j = D_j - O_j - (W_j - p_j) / r_on and the rescue slack S_j = R_j - t. The job is considered spot-eligible only while S_j is large enough to accommodate one complete checkpoint and a small safety margin epsilon: S_j >= C_j + epsilon. Before each spot attempt, the controller selects the cheapest available spot zone from a periodically refreshed table of observed spot prices and revocation rates; this table is used only for cost optimization, not for deadline reasoning. The selected agent loads the latest DMTCP checkpoint, or starts from scratch if p_j is zero, and returns to the scheduler once ready. The scheduler then grants a spot lease of length l_j = min(I_max, S_j - C_j - epsilon), where I_max is an optional user-specified maximum uncheckpointed interval. The lease is chosen shorter than the current rescue slack so that, even if the spot instance dies at any time during the lease and all work since the last checkpoint is lost, the previous protected state p_j can still be rescued by an on-demand request made at the moment of death. At lease expiration, the agent is signaled by DMTCP to take a checkpoint; after the checkpoint commits to the durable store, the job wrapper updates p_j through a side-channel progress value, and the controller recomputes R_j and S_j. If S_j remains at least C_j + epsilon, the job may receive another spot lease; otherwise the job is promoted. Promotion is one-way. The controller enters the job into the guaranteed rescue queue sorted by increasing S_j, so the jobs closest to their no-return point are started first. A rescue worker from the guaranteed pool restores the latest committed checkpoint and runs the job to completion; no further spot attempts are made after promotion because doing so would introduce fresh uncheckpointed risk and could cause churn. Preemption handling is event-driven. Each spot agent runs a SpotServe-style watcher that polls cloud revocation metadata. When a revocation notice arrives, the agent immediately commands DMTCP to produce a final checkpoint; if the checkpoint commits before termination, p_j is updated. If no warning is given, the controller heartbeat watchdog detects the dead instance and falls back to the latest committed checkpoint. In either case the controller recomputes S_j from the protected state and the current wall-clock time. If S_j >= C_j + epsilon and spot capacity remains, the controller launches another lease, preferably in a different zone after a zone revocation; otherwise it performs an on-demand promotion from the same protected state. During the rescue handoff the controller does not count speculative work that was not committed, because the deadline guarantee is based only on protected progress. To keep the system practical, the controller profiles C_j and O_j for each job and instance type, and all checkpoint metadata is stored transactionally with a monotonically increasing version number so that a delayed or partial snapshot cannot corrupt the protected progress. The main tunable parameters are epsilon, which absorbs scheduler delays and clock skew; I_max, which caps checkpointing overhead for very long jobs; and the number of guaranteed rescue workers, which must satisfy the admission check that the aggregate worst-case on-demand execution of accepted jobs can be started before their respective deadlines. This design allows deadline-bound workloads to spend most of their time on 3 to 10 times cheaper spot instances and reserves on-demand execution for the inevitable moments when spot capacity disappears faster than checkpoint-protected progress has accumulated.
